newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: No news on fighting near Pol Pot hideout-military.
newsitem.headline: No news on fighting near Pol Pot hideout-military.

text.p: Cambodian military officials said on Sunday that they had little fresh information on reports of fighting around the northern stronghold of reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot.
Senior military officials said on Saturday that 1,000 rebels who have broken with Pol Pot had surrounded his position about 20 km (12 miles) east of his stronghold of Anlong Veng.
They reported sporadic fighting had taken place among the divided Khmer Rouge guerrillas in the rough jungle terrain.
"We have not been informed of any new developments," senior military adviser Tom Sombol told Reuters.
He said several senior military officials have been sent to the northern provincial town of Siem Reap, about 125 km (75 miles) from Pol Pot's reported location, to try to update the situation.
"I've heard nothing more about the fighting between Pol Pot's supporters," said another official, General Long Sereyrath.

The remoteness of the area and conflicting reports from the government's two main political factions have made it difficult to determine the status of the battle or the fate of Pol Pot, one of this century's most infamous figures.
Deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay told a news conference on Saturday that Pol Pot was holding at least three senior Khmer Rouge officials as hostages.

Pol Pot had fled Anlong Veng after slaughtering his defence chief and 11 of the man's family members, he said. Nhiek Bun Chhay showed grisly photos of crumpled bodies he identified as defence chief Son Sen, his wife Yun Yat and family members.

While there is consensus in Phnom Penh that the rebels have split and are likely fighting each other, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and others expressed doubt over the reports that Pol Pot had taken top comrades, including the rebel government's president Khieu Samphan, as hostages.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters on Friday that Khieu Samphan was a hostage.
The problem of conflicting reports from the two leaders, who formed a strained coalition government after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, is not unusual.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen have been competing to recruit rebels to their respective sides since the Khmer Rouge began unravelling last August, and analysts said they typically produce information that serves their individual agendas.

Ranariddh is eager to make peace with the guerrillas and forge a planned political alliance with Khieu Samphan, but Hun Sen said on Saturday he wants to let the Khmer Rouge fight it out among themselves.

Reports that Khieu Samphan is a hostage are thought to benefit Ranariddh by making the rebel president appear more moderate than Pol Pot and more palatable to Cambodian voters, who will have to decide between Hun Sen and Ranariddh's parties in elections next year.
More than one million Cambodians died during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule through executions, starvation, disease and overwork.
